ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
ACCPPDE101.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
ACCPPDE101.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
ACCPPDE101.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
BENECON111.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
BENECON111.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
BENECON111.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

HCBGATE101.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
HCBGATE101.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
HCBGATE101.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
HCBGATE101.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
HCBGATE101.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments

ENSGATE101.name: Sustainability Essentials I
ENSGATE101.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
ENSGATE101.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
ENSGATE101.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
ENSGATE101.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
BENGATE102.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
BENGATE102.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
BENGATE102.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

ENSECOL112.name: Conservation Biology
ENSECOL112.profile: Introduces conservation biology through biodiversity loss, its human causes and possible responses. Students examine habitat destruction and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change, disasters and extinction, followed by conservation planning, species management and conservation in altered landscapes. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.
ENSECOL112.description2: This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future generations.
ENSECOL112.topics: Biodiversity and ecosystems; Anthropogenic extinction; Habitat loss and fragmentation; Overharvesting; Invasive species; Climate impacts; Natural and human-caused disasters; Conservation priorities; Endangered-species management; Human-modified landscapes; People and conservation; Conservation-study design and evaluation
ENSECOL112.methods: Threatened-species conservation-status analysis; Assessment of species-protection measures; Evidence-based conservation communication

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
GOSSOCI212.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
GOSSOCI212.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
GOSSOCI212.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

ENSGATE201.name: Sustainability Essentials II
ENSGATE201.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
ENSGATE201.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
ENSGATE201.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
ENSGATE201.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
GOSGATE102.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
GOSGATE102.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
GOSGATE102.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
GOSSOCI111.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
GOSSOCI111.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
GOSSOCI111.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

ENSSUST111.name: Climate Change
ENSSUST111.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
ENSSUST111.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
ENSSUST111.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
ENSSUST111.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

ENSSUST112.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
ENSSUST112.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
ENSSUST112.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
ENSSUST112.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
ENSSUST112.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment

ENSECOL212.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
ENSECOL212.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
ENSECOL212.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
ENSECOL212.topics: Ecology and evolution; Environmental conditions and resources; Climate and life cycles; Ecological niches; Competition and cohabitation; Predation and food webs; Natural selection; Population dynamics; Biodiversity patterns; Ecological succession; Ecosystem energy and matter fluxes; Global cycles; Conservation and human impacts; Ecosystem value
ENSECOL212.methods: Ecological modelling in R; Population-dynamics calculations; Ecosystem energy and matter-flux calculations; Ecological research-project design and analysis

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
ENSDELT312.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
ENSDELT312.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
ENSDELT312.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

ENSECOL312.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
ENSECOL312.profile: Examines how food production can balance human needs with environmental impacts. Students assess current agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry, their effects on biodiversity and ecosystems, and alternative practices and innovations. Aquaculture, alternative animal-protein sources and farming for other industries extend the comparison. A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.
ENSECOL312.description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
ENSECOL312.topics: Agricultural and horticultural systems; Environmental impacts of farming; Wildlife and biodiversity; Modification of current farming practices; Alternative agricultural approaches; Animal husbandry; Aquaculture; Alternative protein sources; Farming for non-food industries; Sustainable-farming innovation
ENSECOL312.methods: Scientific-literature review; Comparative appraisal of farming practices and innovations

ENSSUST315.name: Spatial Planning
ENSSUST315.description2: Explores spatial engineering and geospatial technologies like GIS and remote sensing for addressing global challenges such as natural disasters, food shortages, resource decline and pollution. Emphasises hands‑on projects in disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring.

ENSECOL211.name: The Science of Evolution
ENSECOL211.profile: Examines evolutionary theory from genetic mechanisms to the diversification and history of life. Students study natural selection, variation and drift, population and quantitative genetics, adaptation and sexual reproduction, then species concepts, speciation, phylogeny and macroevolution. Genomics, development, biogeography and coevolution extend the account across scales. A project reconstructs a chosen species' evolutionary history using Tinbergen's four questions.
ENSECOL211.description2: Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics, variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life. The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in fields like human health and climate change.
ENSECOL211.topics: Evidence for evolution; Molecular and Mendelian genetics; Natural selection and genetic drift; Multilocus and quantitative genetics; Adaptation and units of selection; Sexual reproduction; Species concepts and speciation; Phylogeny and classification; Evolutionary biogeography; Evolutionary genomics and development; Coevolution; Evolutionary rates, extinction and radiation
ENSECOL211.methods: Evolutionary-history analysis using Tinbergen's four questions; Phylogenetic reconstruction

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
GOSPOLI311.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
GOSPOLI311.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
GOSPOLI311.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis

ENSECOL311.name: Marine Biology
ENSECOL311.profile: Examines marine ecological processes, ocean systems and human impacts on the sea. Physical and chemical oceanography support the study of primary and secondary production, microbial ecology, and habitats from estuaries and shores to the open ocean, deep sea and polar regions. Student seminars address fisheries, aquaculture, acidification, sea-level rise and plastic pollution. A multimedia outreach project translates a marine biological topic for a public audience.
ENSECOL311.description2: Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.
ENSECOL311.topics: Physical and chemical oceanography; Primary and secondary production; Marine microbial ecology; Estuaries; Rocky and sandy shores; Pelagic and continental-shelf ecosystems; Deep-sea ecosystems; Mangroves and seagrass; Coral reefs; Polar marine environments; Fisheries and aquaculture; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Marine plastic pollution

ENSDELT311.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
ENSDELT311.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
ENSDELT311.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
ENSDELT311.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
ENSDELT311.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
BENECON311.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
BENECON311.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
BENECON311.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.description2: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

ENSSUST311.name: Renewable System Design
ENSSUST311.description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
GOSPOLI111.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
GOSPOLI111.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice
GOSPOLI111.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.profile: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
MCCLITR111.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
MCCLITR111.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
MCCLITR111.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

GOSHIST112.name: Histories of Gender
GOSHIST112.profile: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
GOSHIST112.description2: Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
GOSHIST112.topics: Gender and intersectionality; Body sovereignty; Heteronormativity and compulsory heterosexuality; Homonationalism; Rainbow capitalism; Masculinity and sexuality; Queer ageing and memory; Slavery and racialized gender histories; Family and socialization; Health and pathologization; Media bias and book bans; Incarceration; Queer activism and resistance
GOSHIST112.methods: Historical primary-source research; Intersectional analysis; Oral-history interviewing; Critical interpretation of memoir and cultural representations; Arts-based research; Community-engaged activist art; Reflective analysis

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
GOSPHIL212.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
GOSPHIL212.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
GOSPHIL212.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.profile: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.
MCCLITR112.description2: Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.
MCCLITR112.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
MCCLITR112.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
GOSPOLI212.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
GOSPOLI212.topics: International state system and non-state actors; Classical and contemporary geopolitics; Realism and neorealism; Liberalism and neoliberalism; Marxism and world-systems theory; Constructivism and critical theory; Foreign-policy decision-making; War and great-power competition; Colonialism and economic relations; Climate politics; UN Security Council diplomacy
GOSPOLI212.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
GOSPOLI112.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
GOSPOLI112.topics: Democracy and authoritarianism; Democratization and democratic backsliding; States, nations and nationalism; Constitutions and courts; Executives, legislatures and bureaucracies; Political economy; Parties and party systems; Populism and technocracy; Elections and electoral systems; Political culture and polarization; Political participation; Interest groups and public policy
GOSPOLI112.methods: Theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; Concept operationalization and democracy measurement; V-Dem data analysis; Comparative case analysis; Academic literature searching with OpenAlex and AI tools; Empirical election analysis; Research-question formulation

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
GOSHIST111.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
GOSHIST111.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
GOSHIST111.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.profile: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
MCCHEAM111.description2: Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences.
MCCHEAM111.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context
MCCHEAM111.methods: Close visual analysis of paintings; Composition, space, form, tone and colour analysis; On-site artwork study; Historical contextualization; Art-historical text analysis

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.profile: Introduces public international law through its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic legal systems. Legal principles are applied to responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection. The later course examines self-determination, Third World approaches, soft law, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises develop legal reasoning, while a research podcast critically investigates a political dimension of international law.
GOSLAWJ212.description2: Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
GOSLAWJ212.topics: Sources and theories of international law; Treaty law; International legal subjects; Jurisdiction and immunities; Domestic courts and international law; State responsibility; Use of force; UN reform; Armed conflict and international criminal law; International human rights and economic law; Environmental law; Self-determination; Third World Approaches to International Law; Soft law, compliance and effectiveness; Global environmental treaties
GOSLAWJ212.methods: Identification and interpretation of international legal instruments; Judgment and case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to factual scenarios; Legal, empirical and normative critique; Research podcast development

MCCLITR212.name: Life & Travel Writing
MCCLITR212.profile: Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Memory, experience, identity, embodiment and agency frame debates about autobiographical truth, fiction, ethics, trauma and cultural positioning. Close readings connect popular, intellectual and migrant memoirs to theory. Students apply analytical concepts in a personal writing portfolio and an independent comparative or focused life-narrative project.
MCCLITR212.description2: Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.
MCCLITR212.topics: Autobiography and memoir culture; Fact, fiction and autobiographical truth; Autobiographical pact; Self and multiple identities; Individual and collective memory; Experience, embodiment and agency; Ethics and traumatic memory; Grief and disability narratives; Popular memoir and narrative technique; Digital self-presentation; Travel and spiritual self-fashioning; Migration, language and cultural identity
MCCLITR212.methods: Close life-narrative analysis; Smith and Watson's strategies for reading life narratives; Theory-guided analysis of memory, identity, embodiment and agency; Comparative textual and contextual interpretation; Structured autobiographical creative writing

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.description2: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

GOSLAWJ311.name: Principles of Private Law
GOSLAWJ311.profile: Examines property, tort and contract law through comparison of legal systems, primarily Germany, France, England, China and the United States. Students analyze rights and obligations, ownership, nuisance, negligence, contract formation and fairness, remedies and related policy pressures. Legal issue briefs apply the IRAC method. An issue-based comparative contract-law paper and simulated mediation develop comparative analysis, legal argument and negotiation.
GOSLAWJ311.description2: Examines principles of property law, tort law, contract law and other fields within private law. Uses comparisons of legal systems in four countries to explore rights and obligations arising from daily interactions.
GOSLAWJ311.topics: Possession and ownership; Nuisance and property restrictions; Easements, covenants and servitudes; Necessity; Tort structure, intent and negligence; Duties to act; Offer and acceptance; Pre-contractual liability and mistake; Contract fairness and excuse; Specific performance and damages; Unjust enrichment; Mediation and dispute resolution; Private law and public policy
GOSLAWJ311.methods: Functional comparative legal analysis; IRAC legal briefing; Case-law analysis; Application of doctrine to hypothetical facts; Comparative contract-law research; Mediation-position drafting; Simulated mediation and negotiation

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
GOSSOCI311.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
GOSSOCI311.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
GOSSOCI311.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
MCCMEDI311.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
MCCMEDI311.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
MCCMEDI311.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

GOSLAWJ312.name: Foundations of European Union Law
GOSLAWJ312.profile: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.
GOSLAWJ312.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
GOSLAWJ312.topics: European integration and institutions; EU legal sources and fundamental rights; Competences, subsidiarity and proportionality; Supremacy; Direct and indirect effect; State liability; Preliminary rulings; Review of EU acts and enforcement; EU citizenship; Free movement of persons, workers and goods; Establishment and services; Digital-market regulation and green transition
GOSLAWJ312.methods: EU legal-source research; Case-law analysis; Comparative interpretation of EU and national law; Application of free-movement principles to factual scenarios; Structured legal problem analysis

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
GOSPOLI313.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
GOSPOLI313.topics: Conflict theories and structural violence; Identity and historical grievances; Colonialism and forced migration; International peace and security; Humanitarian law and human rights; Positive, negative and hybrid peace; Local peacebuilding; Frozen conflicts; Counterterrorism and rule of law; Transitional justice; Gender and conflict; Development and peacebuilding; Reconciliation, arts and religion; Global South perspectives; Travelling concepts and researcher positionality
GOSPOLI313.methods: Interdisciplinary Research Process; Cross-disciplinary travelling-concept analysis; Conflict case analysis; Context and stakeholder mapping; Annotated bibliography and evidence synthesis; Policy-option appraisal; Policy-brief and background-dossier development; Researcher positionality analysis; Comparative research podcast production

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.description2: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

HCBGATE102.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
HCBGATE102.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
HCBGATE102.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
HCBGATE102.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
HCBGATE102.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

HCBBIOM111.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
HCBBIOM111.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
HCBBIOM111.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
HCBBIOM111.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
HCBBIOM111.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development

HCBLIFE211.name: Molecular Cell Biology
HCBLIFE211.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
HCBLIFE211.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
HCBLIFE211.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
HCBLIFE211.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis

HCBCOGN112.name: Neurobiology
HCBCOGN112.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
HCBCOGN112.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
HCBCOGN112.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
HCBCOGN112.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

HCBLIFE212.name: Human Physiology
HCBLIFE212.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
HCBLIFE212.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
HCBLIFE212.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
HCBLIFE212.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision

HCBLIFE213.name: Biochemistry
HCBLIFE213.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
HCBLIFE213.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
HCBLIFE213.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
HCBLIFE213.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review

HCBPSYC211.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
HCBPSYC211.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
HCBPSYC211.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
HCBPSYC211.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
HCBPSYC211.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting

HCBPSYC212.name: Psychopathology
HCBPSYC212.profile: Examines mental health and psychopathology across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial perspective. Historical views, classification and assessment frame biological, psychological, cultural and social explanations of disorders and treatment. Case-based work applies diagnostic concepts to varied presentations. A structured literature-based essay investigates a focused mental-health question through explicit searching, source selection, evidence appraisal and synthesis, with optional use of PRISMA reporting tools.
HCBPSYC212.description2: The Psychopathology course offers a deep dive into the factors shaping mental health across the lifespan. Students will develop critical thinking skills, explore the bio-psycho-social approach, and gain a comprehensive understanding of mental health and its disorders. Through key concepts, research findings, and psychological assessment techniques, this course empowers individuals to promote wellness and make a meaningful impact in both personal and professional spheres.
HCBPSYC212.topics: Mental-disorder concepts and stigma; Historical and contemporary psychopathology; Biopsychosocial causation; Clinical assessment and diagnostic classification; Stress and health; Anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders; Mood disorders; Somatic and dissociative disorders; Psychotic disorders; Eating and personality disorders; Substance-related and neurocognitive disorders; Sexuality and mental health; Childhood and adolescent disorders; Forensic psychology; Culture and emotion regulation
HCBPSYC212.methods: Diagnostic case analysis; Application and critique of DSM criteria; Biopsychosocial case formulation; Structured literature searching and screening; Source-quality appraisal; Evidence synthesis; Critical evaluation of etiological and intervention models

HCBLIFE214.name: Life Science Laboratory
HCBLIFE214.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
HCBLIFE214.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
HCBLIFE214.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
HCBLIFE214.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation

HCBCOGN212.name: Perception & Action
HCBCOGN212.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

HCBPSYC314.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
HCBPSYC314.profile: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
HCBPSYC314.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
HCBPSYC314.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
HCBPSYC314.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports

HCBLIFE311.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
HCBLIFE311.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
HCBLIFE311.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
HCBLIFE311.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
HCBLIFE311.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis

HCBCOGN311.name: Higher Order Functions
HCBCOGN311.profile: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
HCBCOGN311.description2: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
HCBCOGN311.topics: Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Brain structure and hemispheric specialization; Attention and attentional blink; Memory and long-term potentiation; Emotion; Cognitive control and executive functions; Social cognition; Pain; Consciousness; Brain-behaviour relationships; Neuroscience research ethics
HCBCOGN311.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review

HCBPSYC311.name: Medical & Health Psychology
HCBPSYC311.profile: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
HCBPSYC311.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
HCBPSYC311.topics: Biopsychosocial model; Health inequalities; Health-risk and protective behaviours; Behaviour-change models; Prevention; Stress and coping; Symptom perception; Somatic symptom disorders; Medical consultation; Shared decision-making; Doctor–patient communication; Pain; Chronic illness; Family and caregiver experiences; Quality of life; Cultural competence; Support for healthcare professionals
HCBPSYC311.methods: Psychological case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of health-psychology research and interventions; Clinical-health case formulation; Interviewing-skills practice; Cultural Formulation Interview analysis

HCBBIOM311.name: Pharmacology
HCBBIOM311.profile: Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.
HCBBIOM311.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
HCBBIOM311.topics: Drug discovery and targets; Drug-receptor interactions; Pharmacodynamics; Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; Pharmacokinetics; Antimicrobial therapy; Inflammation and immunopharmacology; Autonomic regulation; Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Pharmacogenomics; Drug toxicity; Access to experimental treatments and evidence; Homeopathy
HCBBIOM311.methods: Concentration-response modelling; Pharmacokinetic time-concentration and time-response analysis; Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameter calculation; Virtual organ-bath experiments; Hypothesis and experimental-design development

HCBPSYC312.name: Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies
HCBPSYC312.profile: Introduces clinical psychological assessment and major psychotherapeutic approaches across the lifespan. Students study ethics, diagnostic systems, test reliability and validity, interviews, personality and cognitive assessment, then psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, systemic and integrative treatments. Training sessions develop introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A psychodiagnostic case report integrates findings and treatment recommendations, while self-monitoring examines developing clinical skills.
HCBPSYC312.description2: Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.
HCBPSYC312.topics: Clinical attitude and ethics; Diagnostic classification; Reliability and validity; Clinical interviews; Personality inventories and projective techniques; Cognitive and neuropsychological assessment; Behavioural and biological assessment; Psychological reporting; Psychodynamic and behavioural therapies; Cognitive therapy and CBT; Person-centered and family therapies; Integrative psychotherapy; Treatment outcomes and evidence; Child and adolescent clinical psychology
HCBPSYC312.methods: Clinical interviewing practice; Introductory psychological-test administration, scoring and interpretation; Psychometric appraisal; Behavioural observation; Integration of assessment data; Psychodiagnostic report writing; Clinical case and therapy-session analysis; Reflective monitoring of clinical skills

HCBBIOM312.name: Infection & Immunity
